story: Anchorage Assembly weighs a $600,000 Real Time Crime Center equipment contract alongside an ordinance that would require Assembly approval before AI powered tracking or identification technology is added

claims.claim: A public hearing on the Real Time Crime Center items is scheduled for the Anchorage Assembly's September 1st meeting.
claims.verbatim: A public hearing is scheduled for the Assembly's Sept. 1 meeting.

claims.claim: The Anchorage Assembly is considering a roughly $600,000 contract with ThunderCat Technology to buy new equipment for the Anchorage Police Department's Real Time Crime Center on Elmore Road.
claims.verbatim: the Anchorage Assembly considered a $600,000 contract with a company called ThunderCat Technology to purchase new equipment for the police department's relatively new Real-Time Crime Center on Elmore Road.

claims.claim: The money for the ThunderCat contract comes from federal and state fine and forfeiture funds.
claims.verbatim: The money for the contract comes from federal and state fine and forfeiture funds.

claims.claim: The proposed upgrade would add video displays, sound equipment and video processing technology to the crime center.
claims.verbatim: the current proposed upgrade would add additional video displays, sound equipment, and video processing technology.

claims.claim: The Anchorage Assembly approved $11.8 million last year for the Real Time Crime Center system.
claims.verbatim: The Assembly last year approved $11.8 million for a new system designed to stream up to 750 camera feeds, automatic license plate readers and drone footage.

claims.claim: Assembly member Sydney Scout describes the Real Time Crime Center as a $12 million commitment made by the Assembly last September.
claims.verbatim: a $12 million commitment made by the Assembly last September
claims.source_outlet: Anchorage Daily News opinion, by Assembly member Sydney Scout

claims.claim: The system is designed to stream up to 750 camera feeds along with automatic license plate readers and drone footage.
claims.verbatim: a new system designed to stream up to 750 camera feeds, automatic license plate readers and drone footage

claims.claim: The camera network the crime center can draw on includes more than 250 city traffic cameras as well as officer worn cameras.
claims.verbatim: That includes the more than 250 traffic cameras around the city, as well as officer-worn cameras

claims.claim: Roughly 216 residents have registered their home security cameras with the police department so far.
claims.verbatim: Roughly 216 residents have registered their home security cameras so far, the newsletter said.

claims.claim: Residents and businesses register their own cameras with the police department voluntarily.
claims.verbatim: cameras owned by residents and businesses who choose to register their cameras with APD

claims.claim: When the Real Time Crime Center launched in September 2025 it ran with one employee and about 15 cameras at police properties and Town Square Park.
claims.verbatim: When it launched in September, the center operated on a small scale, with one employee and about 15 cameras located at APD properties and Town Square Park.

claims.claim: Patrol car license plate records collected through the Real Time Crime Center are destroyed after 14 days unless attached to a criminal case.
claims.verbatim: Patrol car license plate records collected through the Real-Time Crime Center are destroyed after 14 days unless it's attached to a criminal case, he said.

claims.claim: Traffic camera footage is overwritten every three to five days and is not stored unless it is evidence attached to a criminal case.
claims.verbatim: Every three to five days, it is overwritten and not stored unless it is evidence attached to a criminal case, the Real-Time Crime Center overview states.

claims.claim: The proposed ordinance would require a case number for each surveillance data search.
claims.verbatim: Under the proposed ordinance, a case number is required for each surveillance data search.

claims.claim: The proposed ordinance would require the city to erase individuals' data after two weeks unless police are using it as evidence in an active investigation.
claims.verbatim: The city would be required to erase individuals' data after two weeks unless police are using it as evidence in an active investigation

claims.claim: The proposed ordinance would prevent the city from sharing footage with out of state or federal agencies without a warrant.
claims.verbatim: the city would be prevented from sharing footage with out-of-state or federal agencies without a warrant

claims.claim: Co-sponsor Sydney Scout writes that under the ordinance Assembly approval is required before adding new surveillance capabilities including AI powered tracking or identification technology.
claims.verbatim: Assembly approval is required before adding new surveillance capabilities, including AI-powered tracking or identification technology.
claims.source_outlet: Anchorage Daily News opinion, by Assembly member Sydney Scout

claims.claim: Alaska Public Media reports the ordinance would require that the crime center's use of AI be approved by the Assembly.
claims.verbatim: and that the crime center's use of A.I. be approved by the Assembly.

claims.claim: The Anchorage Daily News reports the ordinance would prevent the police department from adding artificial intelligence technology with human feature recognition capabilities without Assembly permission.
claims.verbatim: The ordinance would also prevent the police department from adding artificial intelligence technology with human-feature recognition capabilities into the network without Assembly permission.

claims.claim: The three published accounts describe the ordinance's AI provision in three different ways and the ordinance text itself was not publicly reachable to settle the wording.
claims.verbatim: The ordinance would also prevent the police department from adding artificial intelligence technology with human-feature recognition capabilities into the network without Assembly permission.
claims.source_outlet: Anchorage Daily News, compared against Alaska Public Media and the sponsor's op-ed

claims.claim: In 2023 the Anchorage Assembly placed strict limits on the city's use of facial recognition technology for surveillance.
claims.verbatim: In 2023, the Assembly placed strict limits on the city's use of facial recognition technology for surveillance.

claims.claim: Alaska's News Source reports the Assembly voted to bar the use of facial recognition in 2023.
claims.verbatim: The Assembly voted to bar the use of facial recognition in 2023

claims.claim: Co-sponsor Sydney Scout states that Anchorage already has a ban on facial recognition technology.
claims.verbatim: Anchorage already has a ban on facial recognition technology.
claims.source_outlet: Anchorage Daily News opinion, by Assembly member Sydney Scout

claims.claim: Police Chief Sean Case said the Anchorage Police Department does use object recognition for its license plate readers.
claims.verbatim: Case said APD does use object recognition for their license plate readers.

claims.claim: Chief Sean Case said the police department has some capability to use object recognition with the camera feeds it takes in and that it is unknown whether transmitting that data through the system is possible.
claims.verbatim: And although the police department has 'some capability' to use object recognition with the camera feeds ingested into the Real-Time Crime Center, it's unknown if transmitting that data through its system is possible, he said.

claims.claim: Chief Sean Case said the police department does not use facial recognition technology.
claims.verbatim: The police department does not use that technology, Case said.

claims.claim: Chief Sean Case said some of those technologies come with the equipment the department has and that before using any of them the department will come to the Assembly body generally through the Public Health and Safety Committee.
claims.verbatim: Some of those types of technologies come with the equipment that we have. And prior to using any of those sorts of pieces of technology, we will come to the body generally in the form of the Public Health and Safety Committee

claims.claim: Chief Sean Case said the technology package is a very significant move for the municipality and that the department is not going to outrun its coverage on it.
claims.verbatim: It's a very significant move for the municipality. It's our response to crime. We think it's going to have a significant impact, but we are not going to outrun our coverage on this

claims.claim: Assembly member Keith McCormick said Anchorage code can't answer his constituents' questions about what is collected, who can see it and how long it is kept.
claims.verbatim: When my constituents ask, 'What are we collecting? Who can see it? How long do we keep it?' Anchorage code can't answer any of those questions. We have no legislative guardrails.

claims.claim: Assembly member Sydney Scout said Alaskans have a right to privacy that shall not be infringed and that the sponsors are trying to enshrine existing rights into the new system.
claims.verbatim: It's very clear that we have a right to privacy that shall not be infringed in Alaska. So we're both trying to get ahead of future concerns and trying to enshrine the existing rights and civil liberties that we have in Alaska into this new system.

claims.claim: Assembly member Sydney Scout said the proposed license plate reader policy would allow use only for traffic enforcement and justifiable tracking reasons like missing kids or stolen vehicles.
claims.verbatim: What we're proposing in our policy around license plate reader technology is that it is really only used for traffic enforcement and for justifiable tracking reasons like missing kids or stolen vehicles.

claims.claim: Assembly member Sydney Scout said the sponsors want the protections in code now so that they hold when the political winds shift and no matter who oversees the system.
claims.verbatim: Let's put this into code now, so that when power changes, when the political winds shift, as they always do, we have protections for the people, no matter who is overseeing and implementing the system.

claims.claim: Chief Sean Case said the Real Time Crime Center is a separate entity from dispatch and that its resources are used after a call comes in to help officers respond.
claims.verbatim: The Real-Time Crime Center is a separate entity from dispatch. And so what they're going to use is once a call comes into dispatch center, then they're going to utilize these resources to help officers to respond to the call.

claims.claim: Keith McCormick, Sydney Scout and Vice Chair Daniel Volland introduced the surveillance ordinance at the Assembly's meeting on Tuesday, August 18th.
claims.verbatim: On Tuesday, McCormick, member Sydney Scout and Vice Chair Daniel Volland introduced an ordinance that would set new restrictions on automatic license plate readers and live camera monitoring and limit the retention of surveillance data.

claims.claim: Keith McCormick raised his concerns at an August 4th Assembly meeting and asked that approval of the contract be postponed, a request Sydney Scout agreed with.
claims.verbatim: member Keith McCormick said during an Aug. 4 Assembly meeting

claims.claim: The Assembly held a work session on the Real Time Crime Center on Friday, August 21st.
claims.verbatim: The Assembly will hold a work session on the Real-Time Crime Center on Friday at 10:40 a.m.

killed.claim: The ThunderCat contract is a three-year contract.
killed.why: No fetched page establishes a contract term.

killed.claim: Axon is the platform vendor for the Real Time Crime Center.
killed.why: Axon appears only in an ADN photo caption describing a body camera. Unsupported.

killed.claim: The ordinance would give newly added surveillance technology a temporary approval status and require annual reporting.
killed.why: No verbatim sentence recoverable on re-fetch.

killed.claim: The Assembly postponed the contract vote on August 18th.
killed.why: Wrong date. The postponement request was August 4th.

killed.claim: The ordinance was introduced on August 4th.
killed.why: Wrong date. August 4th is the meeting where McCormick objected to the contract; the ordinance was introduced Tuesday August 18th.

killed.claim: Chief Sean Case said the department has never tested facial recognition.
killed.why: No page carries this. Only 'does not use' is supported.

killed.claim: The Real Time Crime Center currently runs AI identification of people.
killed.why: Contradicted by the record. The AI in the system today is plate reading.

killed.claim: Human feature recognition is the ordinance's own wording.
killed.why: Traceable only to the ADN reporter's sentence. Ordinance text unobtainable.

killed.claim: The ordinance carries AO number X.
killed.why: No AO number printed on any page; municipal systems would not yield one.

killed.claim: Sydney Scout said she would not have approved the initial Real Time Crime Center.
The 2023 measure is a flat ban on facial recognition that is still in force.
killed.why: Outlets disagree on strength. Split into C21, C22 and C23 rather than shipped whole.

notes: ORDINANCE TEXT NOT FOUND. anchorage.legistar.com returned 'Invalid parameters' and muni.org carried no September 1st 2026 agenda, so no AO number exists in this file. Every description of the ordinance here is a description by a journalist or by the sponsor, never the statutory text, and no slide may present any of it inside quotation marks as the ordinance's language. THREE PRIMARY CLAIMS, C06, C17 and C23, all from Sydney Scout's signed op-ed, the co-sponsor writing about her own ordinance. THE AI PROVISION: use C17, the sponsor's own wording, the only formulation consistent with all three accounts. Print 'human feature recognition' only with explicit ADN attribution, or not at all. THE LIMITING FACT: the Real Time Crime Center is not an AI identification system today. It reads plates with object recognition, the chief says it does not use facial recognition, and the chief says it is unknown whether object recognition data can even be transmitted through the system. FIGURE HYGIENE: $11.8 million (C05) and Scout's '$12 million commitment' (C06) are the same money described twice, never print both. 750 feeds (C07) is design capacity; about 15 cameras with one employee (C11) is the launch state; that contrast is the honest spine. The 14 day plate retention (C12) and three to five day traffic overwrite (C13) are CURRENT practice and not code, which is why the two week deletion rule (C15) is proposed. TIMELINE: August 4th McCormick objects and asks to postpone; August 18th the ordinance is introduced; August 21st work session; September 1st public hearing.
